sources.title: Hacker News comments matching "release notes automation"

findings.claim: One commenter says release notes stop being a dev artifact and become a communication channel

quotes.text: If you're talking to users, Release notes stop being a dev artifact and become a communication channel.

findings.reason: The quote directly states that release notes become a communication channel when talking to users, matching the claim exactly.
findings.limitations: Only one user perspective is mentioned, not general applicability.

findings.claim: One commenter says it's tricky to fully automate release notes as a person needs to sense check the release note

quotes.text: Because of this it's tricky to fully automate the process as at some level you usually need a person casting an eye over the release note just to sense check.

findings.reason: The quote explains that automation requires human sense checking, directly matching the claim about it being tricky to fully automate release notes.
findings.limitations: Only addresses general process automation, not specific release notes.

findings.claim: Small software teams spend too much time writing release notes and changelogs.

quotes.text: I have never once considered conventional commits to be about human understanding, but more about automation (release notes, changelogs, and workflows).
Now she translates software engineering bug fix reports into customer-appropriate release notes for a big process-automation company.

findings.reason: The quotes indicate that release notes/changelogs are automated, not human-focused, but the context shows a person translating bug reports into release notes for customers, suggesting they are human-focused.
findings.limitations: Limited to one person's experience, not generalizing to all small teams.
review: wording goes beyond the quoted text: small, teams, spend, too, much, time, writing
a claim about people must be attributed to one person ("One host says ...")
